titleZh: 冬季消防检查陆续开始，酒店先自查哪几处、整改怎么留证据？
titleEn: Winter Fire Safety Inspections Are Underway: Where Should Hotels Check First, and How Should They Document Rectification?
summaryZh: 冬季消防检查前，酒店先查员工宿舍取暖器、电动自行车停放充电、厨房燃气和常闭防火门四处后场。当班不用外部单位、不用申请费用就能恢复安全的当场改，其余列入四列整改台账限期改并做临时措施。难在留证：改前改后同角度对照、两层签认、非整改人在夜班或交接时段复查、记录闭环时间。外部事实只引山东、四川两地材料。
summaryEn: Before winter fire safety inspections, hotels should check heaters in staff accommodation, electric-bicycle parking and charging, kitchen gas systems, and fire doors designed to stay closed. Correct what the duty team can make safe immediately; track other items in a four-column hazard log with interim controls, sign-offs, independent reinspection and closure dates.
contentZh:
冬季消防检查陆续开始，酒店先自查哪几处、整改怎么留证据？

冬季消防检查前，酒店先查后场四处：员工宿舍的取暖器、电动自行车停放充电、厨房燃气、常闭防火门。查出的问题分两类：当班在场的人不用外部单位、不用申请费用就能恢复安全状态的，当场改，并留下改后记录；其余写进隐患台账，定下整改责任人、期限和复查证据，由整改人以外的人复查通过才算关闭。难点在后一半：自查找到问题不难，证明它改好了、而且没有再犯，才难。

这篇写给单体酒店的总经理和工程负责人。下面先看两地近期的检查说明了什么，再说为什么先查后场、怎样区分当场改和限期改并填一张整改台账，最后讲证据怎样留、谁来签。

冬季消防检查会查什么？

从山东和四川两份近期材料看，检查既看隐患本身，也看查出后有没有责任人、期限和复查。它们是地区材料，不代表全国统一要求。

山东省消防救援局2026年11月11日发布《关于加强冬季火灾防控工作的通告》，要求全省各单位按“消防安全检查日”机制组织防火巡查检查，重点检查违规用火用电、电气线路老化、消防设施缺失或停用、占用堵塞疏散通道和安全出口、电动自行车进楼入户等问题；通告还写明，禁止在建筑物的公共门厅、疏散通道、楼梯间、安全出口等公共区域停放电动自行车或者为电动自行车及其电池充电。通告后附的倡议面向居民，提醒取暖设备与窗帘、被褥等可燃物保持安全距离，燃气要定期检查软管和阀门。

人民网四川频道2026年11月14日报道，四川冕宁县消防救援局11月13日联合多个部门督导检查人员密集场所，在酒店抽查了客房防烟面罩配备和厨房燃气安全。对检查中发现的疏散通道堆物、常闭式防火门未保持关闭等问题，督导组当场责令立即整改；消防设施损坏等难以当场整改的隐患，建立隐患清单，明确整改责任人与期限，跟踪督办到闭环销号。报道还说，下一步将用“回头看”和错时夜查复查验收，防止隐患回潮。

这两份材料能说明当地的检查重点和处理方式，说明不了别的地区会查什么、查到什么程度。报道里列的问题出自多类受检场所，不能读成都是酒店的问题。本文判断，冕宁“当场改、列清单、回头看”的做法，正好可以拿来做酒店内部的整改规矩：外部复查来的时候，酒店需要拿得出同样的东西。

为什么先查后场这四处？

前场有客人和巡查经过，问题容易被看见；后场只有员工进出，同一个问题改了又犯，常常没人发现。本文判断，这四处都容易回潮。

宿舍里的取暖器如果是员工自己买的，收走一台不难，难的是宿舍冷，收了还会再出现；插线板串接、取暖器离被褥太近，也多发生在夜里，白天查不到。电动自行车也是这样：今天把车从楼梯间推出去，明天没有别的地方充电，车还会回来。厨房燃气的风险藏在软管、阀门和报警装置里，平时看不出，要按时查。常闭防火门容易被一块木楔、一个垃圾桶撑开，往往是为了推车进出方便。

所以，后场四处要同时查两件事：现场此刻是否安全，导致它回潮的原因有没有处理。

当场能改和限期整改怎么分？

当班在场的人不用外部单位、不用申请费用，就能恢复安全状态的，当场改；其余列入台账限期改，期限内先做临时措施。

按这条规则，同一处地方可能两类都有。撑开的防火门，关上、拿走木楔，是当场改；闭门器坏了、门扇变形关不严，要报修，是限期改。宿舍里收走自购取暖器、拔掉串接的插线板，是当场改；宿舍取暖不足，要加装合规的取暖设备或改线路，是限期改。楼梯间里的电动自行车推走，是当场改；要设集中停放充电的位置，涉及场地和用电，是限期改。厨房闻到燃气味，当班关阀、停用相关灶具并通知燃气供应单位，是当场的处置；软管更换、报警装置维修，要由燃气单位或具备相应能力的人员完成，归限期。

限期整改不等于期限内照常使用。台账要写明期限内的临时措施，例如防火门修好之前，安排专人在每次交接班时检查是否关闭；燃气设备修好之前停用。

酒店消防自查的整改台账可以只用四列：

隐患｜整改责任人｜期限｜复查证据
常闭防火门被撑开、闭门器损坏｜工程负责人｜撑开的当班关闭；闭门器按报修确认的日期修好，期间每班专人检查｜改前改后同角度照片，维修单，夜班复查记录
员工宿舍使用自购取暖器、插线板串接｜人事行政负责人｜当班收走、断电；宿舍取暖方案定下完成日期｜收缴登记，宿舍夜间复查记录，取暖方案落实凭证
电动自行车在楼梯间停放或充电｜保安负责人｜当班移出；集中停放充电位置定下启用日期｜移出前后照片，复查时同位置照片，充电位置启用凭证
厨房燃气软管老化、报警装置故障｜厨师长与工程负责人｜相关灶具当班停用；按燃气单位确认的日期更换维修｜停用记录，燃气单位或维修单位作业单，复查记录

每一行都按同一条规则拆成两段：当班能恢复的写当班，要外部单位或要申请费用的写约定日期和期间的临时措施。表里的期限只写怎样定，不给天数，天数按本店的维修条件和当地检查要求定。

为什么说整改留证比自查更难？

自查只需要发现问题；留证要证明谁在什么时候改了、改完经不经得住复查，这些都要在发现之后一件件补齐。

第一个难处是改后状态会回潮。上午十点拍一张防火门关着的照片，证明不了晚上十点它还关着。冕宁的复查采用错时夜查，本文理解也是这个道理：白天合格，说明不了夜里也合格。

第二个难处是动手和负责分在不同人手里。燃气维修要外部单位做，宿舍归人事行政，电动自行车归保安，门和线路归工程。每个人都动过一点，到复查时却没有一个人能说清这条隐患关了没有。

第三个难处是期限没人追。限期整改最常见的结局是一直在办：维修单位排期、配件没到、预算还在批，时间一长，台账上的日期就失去意义。

所以留证的规矩要在自查之前定好。查之前先说清每类隐患要留什么，比查完再回头补照片可靠。本站讨论云南旅馆治安走查的旧文提过，整改项目要有责任人和关闭证据；下面把这件事落到消防隐患上。

一条隐患的证据要留到什么程度？

一条隐患能关闭，要有改前改后对照、动手人和责任人签认、整改人以外的人复查，以及从发现到关闭的时间。

改前照片和改后照片要同一位置、同一角度，画面里认得出是哪一层、哪扇门，带拍摄时间。只有改后照片，说明不了改了什么。外部单位做的维修，作业单比照片更有用，上面有单位、日期和更换的部件。

签认分两层。动手的人写明做了什么；整改责任人确认这一项可以提交复查。责任人签字，意味着他认这件事归他管，以后同一处再出问题，先找他。

复查由不是整改人的人来做，而且至少有一次放在夜班或交接时段。复查看的是问题有没有回来，所以要回到同一位置、同一角度再拍一次。复查不通过的，这一行不关闭，写上原因，重新定期限。

闭环时间是从发现到复查通过的日期差。它能说明酒店处理隐患快不快，说明不了处理得彻不彻底；彻底与否，要看之后的检查里同一处有没有再出现。同一处关闭后再次出现，就不再按当场改了结，而要列入限期整改去找原因，例如宿舍取暖、充电位置这类根子上的问题。

委托管理、特许加盟和业主自营，谁来签？

日常整改由经营团队做，但逾期和复查不通过的记录，要让对酒店消防安全负总责的人看到。

山东通告写明，各单位法定代表人、主要负责人或实际控制人是本单位消防安全第一责任人。本文建议按这个口径分工：委托管理的酒店，台账由管理方派驻的总经理组织，业主可以要求每月看一次逾期未关的隐患和复查不通过的记录。特许加盟和业主自营的酒店，台账在业主自己的团队手里，由总经理组织，逾期项是否追加预算由业主决定。厨房外包的，燃气一行的整改责任人仍写酒店方的对接人，承包方的作业记录附在后面。具体责任要看合同和当地规定。

怎样先试一轮，什么时候算做到了？

先用一个星期按四处做一轮，看台账能不能让每条隐患都找得到责任人、期限和复查记录。

试之前，总经理和工程负责人先写下判断标准：每一行四列都有内容；限期整改的都写了临时措施；复查人和整改人不是同一人；夜班或交接时段的复查至少一次。试完按这些标准对照，不在试后改标准。

出现下面几种情况，说明这套做法还没立住，要先停下来补：复查人找不到改前照片；同一处在复查时回潮；限期项过了日期没有说明；责任人不认这一行。前两种回到留证要求，后两种回到分工。

这套方法管不到什么？

它只管后场四处的自查和整改留证，不判断建筑本身和消防设施是否合规，也不替代专业检测。

消防设施的维保、电气线路的安全评估、燃气设备的检修，要由具备相应资质或能力的单位完成；前场客房、疏散通道、消防控制室值班和员工培训，本文没有展开。本文引用的是山东和四川的材料，其他地区的检查口径以当地发布为准。迈创兄弟C&T可以协助酒店把整改台账和复查安排落到日常管理里。

contentEn:
Winter Fire Safety Inspections Are Underway: Where Should Hotels Check First, and How Should They Document Rectification?

Before a winter fire safety inspection, hotels should first check four back-of-house areas: heaters in staff accommodation, the parking and charging of electric bicycles, kitchen gas equipment, and fire doors designed to remain closed. Problems fall into two groups. If the staff on duty can restore a safe condition without an outside contractor or a spending request, correct it at once and record the result. Put other issues in a hazard log, assign an owner and a deadline, and specify what evidence will be used for reinspection. An item is closed only after someone other than the person who carried out the repair has checked it and confirmed it passes. The harder part comes after finding a problem: proving that it was fixed and has not returned.

This article is for general managers and engineering leads at individual hotels. It first looks at what two recent local inspection notices tell us, then explains why back-of-house areas deserve early attention, how to distinguish immediate corrections from deadline-based rectification and complete a hazard log, and how to keep evidence and assign sign-offs.

What do winter fire safety inspections check?

Two recent materials from Shandong and Sichuan show that inspections look both at hazards and at whether a responsible person, a deadline and a follow-up check are in place. These are regional materials; they do not establish a nationwide, uniform inspection requirement.

On 11 November 2026, the Shandong Provincial Fire and Rescue Department issued a notice on strengthening winter fire prevention and control. It asks organisations across the province to organise fire patrols and inspections under the “Fire Safety Inspection Day” mechanism, focusing on unauthorised use of fire or electricity, ageing electrical wiring, missing or deactivated fire protection equipment, obstructed evacuation routes and exits, and electric bicycles brought into buildings or homes. It also prohibits parking electric bicycles or charging bicycles and their batteries in shared areas such as building lobbies, evacuation routes, stairwells and safety exits. An accompanying appeal for residents advises keeping heaters at a safe distance from curtains, bedding and other combustible materials, and regularly checking gas hoses and valves.

A report published on 14 November 2026 by People’s Daily Online’s Sichuan channel says that on 13 November the Mianning County Fire and Rescue Bureau, together with several departments, inspected crowded public venues. At a hotel, inspectors checked whether guest rooms had smoke hoods and whether kitchen gas systems were safe. They ordered immediate correction of problems such as stored items blocking evacuation routes and fire doors that should remain closed being left open. Hazards that could not be corrected immediately, such as damaged fire equipment, were entered on a hazard list with a named owner and deadline, then tracked to closure. The report also says follow-up checks would include later visits and inspections at different times, including at night, to prevent hazards from returning.

These materials show local inspection priorities and response methods. They do not tell us what another region will inspect or how far its checks will go. The problems listed in the report arose across several types of inspected venues; they should not be read as problems found only, or all, at hotels. In this article’s assessment, Mianning’s sequence—correct what can be fixed immediately, list the rest and revisit—offers a useful model for a hotel’s internal rectification rules. When an outside inspector returns, the hotel should be able to produce comparable records.

Why check these four back-of-house areas first?

Guests and inspectors pass through front-of-house areas, so problems there are easier to notice. Staff are the only people who usually enter back-of-house areas. The same issue can be fixed and then recur without anyone seeing it. In this article’s assessment, all four areas are prone to recurring hazards.

If an employee bought a heater for a dormitory, taking away one heater is easy; the harder question is whether the room is cold enough that another one will appear. Daisy-chained power strips and heaters placed too close to bedding are also more likely to be used at night and missed during daytime checks. Electric bicycles create a similar cycle: a bicycle removed from a stairwell today may return tomorrow if there is nowhere else to charge it. Gas risks in the kitchen can be hidden in hoses, valves and alarms; they need scheduled checks. A block of wood or a rubbish bin can keep a fire door open, often to make it easier to move carts through.

For each of these four areas, check two things: whether the location is safe now, and whether the cause of recurrence has been addressed.

How do you distinguish an immediate correction from deadline-based rectification?

If the staff on duty can restore a safe condition without an outside contractor or a spending request, correct it immediately. Put other items in the hazard log with a deadline, and take interim measures in the meantime.

A single location may need both kinds of action. If a fire door is propped open, close it and remove the wedge immediately. If its closer is broken or the door is warped so that it will not shut, arrange a repair by a deadline. In a dormitory, remove a heater bought by an employee and unplug daisy-chained power strips at once; providing adequate heating may require an approved heater or electrical work and should be scheduled. Move an electric bicycle out of a stairwell immediately; establishing a designated parking and charging area takes planning and electrical work and should be deadline-based. If gas is smelled in the kitchen, the duty team should close the valve, stop using the affected appliances and notify the gas supplier at once. Replacing a hose or repairing an alarm should be done by the gas supplier or a person with the required capability, by an agreed deadline.

Deadline-based rectification does not mean continuing normal use until the deadline. Record interim controls in the log. For example, until the fire door is repaired, assign someone to check at every shift handover that it is closed. Stop using gas equipment that cannot safely operate while awaiting repair.

A hotel fire-safety self-inspection log can use just four columns:

| Hazard | Rectification owner | Deadline | Reinspection evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fire door propped open; closer damaged | Engineering lead | Close the door during the shift; repair the closer by the date confirmed with the repair provider; assign a person to check each shift in the meantime | Before-and-after photos from the same angle; repair order; night-shift reinspection record |
| Staff dormitory using personally purchased heaters and daisy-chained power strips | HR and administration lead | Collect heaters and disconnect unsafe wiring during the shift; set a completion date for an adequate heating plan | Collection log; night-time dormitory reinspection; evidence that the heating plan is in place |
| Electric bicycle parked or charged in a stairwell | Security lead | Move the bicycle out during the shift; set an opening date for a designated parking and charging area | Photos before and after removal; photo of the same location at reinspection; evidence that the charging area is open |
| Ageing kitchen gas hose; gas alarm malfunction | Head chef and engineering lead | Stop using the affected appliance during the shift; replace or repair it by the date confirmed with the gas or repair provider | Stop-use record; work order from the gas or repair provider; reinspection record |

Each line follows the same split: state what can be made safe during the shift; for work requiring an outside provider or a spending request, set an agreed date and record interim controls. The table explains how to set a deadline, not how many days to allow. Set the time based on the hotel’s repair capacity and local inspection requirements.

Why is documenting rectification harder than finding a hazard?

A self-inspection only needs to identify a problem. Evidence must show who corrected it, when it was corrected and whether it stands up to reinspection. Those details have to be assembled one by one after the hazard is found.

The first challenge is recurrence. A photo of a closed fire door at 10 a.m. does not prove that it is still closed at 10 p.m. Mianning’s follow-up included inspections at different times, including at night. This article reads that as a reminder that passing a daytime check does not show that the same place will pass at night.

The second challenge is that the hands-on work and overall responsibility belong to different people. An outside provider repairs gas systems; HR and administration manage staff accommodation; security handles electric bicycles; engineering handles doors and wiring. Several people may each do part of the work, yet at reinspection no one may be able to say whether the hazard has been closed.

The third challenge is that nobody follows the deadline. Deadline-based rectification can remain “in progress” for too long: the repair provider has a queue, parts have not arrived, or a budget is still being approved. Once enough time has passed, the date in the log no longer means anything.

Set the evidence rules before the self-inspection. Agree in advance what each type of hazard needs as proof; that is more reliable than trying to reconstruct the record afterwards. An earlier article on this site about hotel security checks in Yunnan noted that every rectification item needs an owner and evidence of closure. The following applies that principle to fire-safety hazards.

How much evidence is enough to close one hazard?

To close an item, keep a before-and-after comparison, sign-offs from the person who did the work and the responsible owner, a check by someone other than the person who made the correction, and the dates from discovery through closure.

Take before and after photos from the same location and angle. Make sure the image identifies the floor and door, and retain its capture time. An after photo alone does not show what changed. For work by an outside provider, a service record is more useful than a photo if it names the provider, date and parts replaced.

Use two levels of sign-off. The person who did the work records what was done; the responsible owner confirms that the item is ready for reinspection. By signing, the owner acknowledges responsibility for the item. If the same location becomes hazardous again, that person is the first point of follow-up.

A person other than the one who made the correction should conduct the reinspection. Schedule at least one check during a night shift or handover period. The purpose is to see whether the hazard has returned, so check the same location and take another photo from the same angle. If it fails, leave the item open, record why, and set a new deadline.

Closure time is the number of days from discovery to a successful reinspection. It can show how quickly the hotel handles hazards, but not how thoroughly it resolved them. To assess that, check whether the same location appears again in later inspections. If it does, do not treat the second occurrence as another quick fix. Put it on the deadline-based list and find the underlying cause, such as inadequate dormitory heating or a lack of charging space.

Under a management contract, franchise or owner-operated model, who signs?

The operating team handles routine rectification. Records of overdue items and failed reinspections should also reach the person with overall responsibility for the hotel’s fire safety.

The Shandong notice says that each organisation’s legal representative, principal person in charge or actual controller is the first person responsible for its fire safety. Using that as a reference, this article recommends the following division of work. At a managed hotel, the general manager appointed by the management company organises the log. The owner can ask to review overdue hazards and failed reinspection records monthly. At a franchised or owner-operated hotel, the log stays with the owner’s own team and the general manager organises it; the owner decides whether to add budget for overdue items. If the kitchen is outsourced, name the hotel’s liaison as the owner for the gas item and attach the contractor’s work record. Actual responsibility depends on the contract and local requirements.

How should you run the first cycle, and when is it working?

Use one week to run a first cycle across the four areas. See whether the log lets you find an owner, a deadline and a reinspection record for every item.

Before starting, the general manager and engineering lead should write down the pass criteria: all four columns are completed for every item; every deadline-based item has interim controls; the person re-inspecting is not the person who made the correction; and at least one reinspection takes place on a night shift or at handover. Compare results against these criteria after the trial; do not change the criteria afterwards to make the result look better.

If any of the following happens, the process is not yet established and should be paused for correction: the reinspection owner cannot find the before photo; a hazard returns at reinspection; a deadline passes without an explanation; or the assigned owner does not accept the item. The first two point back to the evidence requirements; the latter two point back to the division of responsibility.

What does this method not cover?

It covers self-inspection and rectification records for these four back-of-house areas. It does not assess whether the building itself or its fire-protection systems comply with applicable requirements, and it does not replace professional testing.

Maintenance of fire-protection systems, safety assessments of electrical wiring, and servicing of gas equipment should be completed by providers with the required qualifications or capabilities. This article does not cover guest rooms and evacuation routes in front-of-house areas, staffing of the fire control room or employee training. It cites materials from Shandong and Sichuan; elsewhere, follow inspection requirements published by the local authorities.
